reviews.one_line_contribution: The claim is that an optimized instruction and a retrieved memory item are informational substitutes at the level of a specific clause-item pair, tested causally by deleting the one instruction clause a retrieved item duplicates and showing that this — but not deleting a length-matched unrelated clause — restores the item's marginal value; the k*-shrinkage grid is the observational wrapper around that mechanism test.
reviews.closest_prior_work: The proposal itself names MemMachine (arXiv:2604.04853) as pre-empting the observation, and correctly retreats to mechanism. The more dangerous neighbour it does not confront is the instruction-vs-demonstration substitution already visible inside the prompt-optimization literature it cites: MIPROv2's own ablations report that instruction optimization and bootstrapped demonstrations are largely non-additive, with instruction search paying off mainly on tasks whose conditional rules the demonstrations fail to convey — which is the substitution claim in the demonstration slot, one abstraction step from this proposal's memory slot. Stack that on Min et al.'s finding that demonstrations contribute format and label space more than content, plus FILCO/RECOMP/MMR redundancy filtering and the lost-in-the-middle distractor line for the harm side, and the conceptual space is crowded enough that the surviving delta is narrow: 'the conditioning variable for redundancy should be the instruction clause, not the query or the other items.' That is a real delta, but it is a refinement, not a new phenomenon, and the proposal argues for it against MemMachine only, never against MIPROv2's non-additivity result.
reviews.strongest_objection: P2, the load-bearing prediction, does not test the claim that makes the paper interesting. E4's DiD compares (B-B0)-(A-A0) against (C-C0)-(A-A0): deleting clause c(m*) removes procedural information from the instruction, and m* re-supplies it. A positive DiD therefore follows from plain additive information accounting — content that supplies missing information helps more when the information is missing — and is close to tautological given how m* is selected (max redundancy against c(m*)). What substitution needs, and what the pilot and the k* story actually assert, is that a duplicated item has *negative* marginal value under the full instruction, i.e. arm A < A0 beyond the noise floor. Sub-additivity down to zero marginal value cannot move argmax-k from {4,8} to {0,1,2}; only a positive interference cost can. The plan never pre-registers a sign test on A-A0, so the 'ceiling/saturation killer' can pass cleanly while the harm claim — the entire motivation — goes untested. A reviewer will also note that if A-A0 is near zero (the likely case, since these are the most redundant items), the DiD reduces to 'B beats A', which is just the confound the placebo arm C was meant to remove being reintroduced through the selection rule.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Four changes, none of which need more budget. (1) Add to P2 a necessary condition: high-R items must show negative marginal value under I3 (A significantly below A0 against the E3 null floor); report the DiD as uninterpretable for the substitution claim if A-A0 >= 0, since a positive DiD with a non-negative A-A0 is ordinary information restoration. (2) Add an instruction-side length placebo to the E1 ladder — I0 padded to I3-s1's token count with non-procedural filler, and/or a clause-scrambled I3 — so the k-slope difference is attributable to procedural content rather than instruction length, position, or specificity. E2 pads the memory but nothing pads the instruction, and I_H controls only for GEPA provenance, not length. (3) Move the MIPROv2 bootstrapped-demonstration arm at matched k out of the conditional Tier 3 and into Tier 1: without it the paper cannot say whether substitution is about self-edited memory or about any in-context exemplar. (4) Run the promised >=15-query search before committing the design, not before submission; and pre-register how uncertainty on argmax-k is computed (bootstrap over items), since 'argmax moved regime' is currently an unquantified conjunct of P1.
reviews.missing_baseline: A length-matched non-procedural instruction (I0 inflated to I3-s1's token count with generic, task-relevant-sounding but non-procedural text) crossed with k, plus a clause-scrambled variant of I3-s1. Every instruction-level contrast in E1 confounds procedural content with instruction length and specificity, and E2's padding is applied to the memory slot only, so nothing in Tier 1 rules out 'longer instructions leave less usable attention for injected context.' Secondary omission: the MIPROv2 bootstrapped-demonstration arm at matched k, which is the control separating 'self-edited memory substitutes for instructions' from 'any demonstrations substitute for instructions', is parked in E8 and runs only if Tiers 1-2 are already positive — i.e. the discriminating control is conditional on the result it is supposed to discriminate.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is, by the proposal's own admission, empty: the search tool failed on every attempt and this round contributes no new collision evidence. Honesty about that is creditable but it is not a substitute for having searched, and per the standard that an unsearched novelty claim is a weakness, this costs the proposal. The carried-forward list comes from an earlier five-query-capped search, and the newest items cited are 2603/2604 identifiers — roughly four to six months stale in a field the proposal itself argues moves in preprint time; the entire recent window is unexamined. I cannot verify any of the cited identifiers here, so the collision status must be read as unknown rather than clear. The named risk is specific and live: if MemMachine or a successor already reports an item-level or clause-level causal probe of the prompt-retrieval interaction, the surviving delta collapses to the noise-floor-referenced effect sizes, which is a workshop-scale contribution. The commitment to re-search before submission is the wrong sequencing — a collision found then invalidates experiments already run, so the search belongs before Tier 1, and the proposal should say so.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A clause-level causal test that the harm from injected episodic memory under an optimized instruction is *relational* — a property of the (instruction clause, memory item) pair rather than a global property of the instruction (length, specificity, ceiling) — together with a noise-floor-referenced estimate of how the accuracy-optimal injection budget k* shrinks as the instruction absorbs procedure.
reviews.closest_prior_work: MemMachine (arXiv:2604.04853), which the proposal itself names: it already reports that prompt design interacts with retrieval depth and that prompt choice changes retrieval's marginal value across depths. That does not fully pre-empt the paper, because MemMachine reports it as an observation and does not localize the effect to specific instruction content. But it does something worse for this particular design: it makes E1/P1 — the *primary* pre-registered claim, the one the grid is powered for and the one that consumes 25 of 76 passes — a replication, while the actually-new contribution (E4's clause knockout) is a 6-pass Tier-2 experiment that the authors themselves rate as their least powerful test. The power budget is spent on the known part. Secondary threats: arXiv:2412.15266 and RAVEN already establish k-plateaus and an upper limit on useful in-context examples (so the existence and rough location of k* is not new), and FILCO/RECOMP/MMR/arXiv:2604.24334 already establish redundancy-based context gating, leaving only the choice of conditioning variable (against the instruction rather than against the query or the other items) as the algorithmic delta.
reviews.strongest_objection: E4, the experiment carrying the entire mechanism claim, is both confounded and underpowered, and each failure alone is enough to sink the paper. (a) Headroom confound: c(m*) is selected as the clause most duplicated by the item retrieved for *this* query, while the placebo c' is selected as a clause that *no* item retrieved for this query duplicates. The two knockouts are therefore not exchangeable by construction — B deletes a query-relevant clause and C deletes a query-irrelevant one. If B0 is even slightly harder than C0, more items are wrong in B0 and are therefore *available to be fixed*, so a single injected item mechanically has larger marginal value under B than under C, yielding DiD > 0 with no relational substitution whatsoever. This is a floor effect, the exact mirror of the ceiling effect the design claims to kill, and the proposed guard — 'we verify B0 vs C0 are indistinguishable within the noise floor' — is a non-inferiority claim adjudicated by failing to reject at a 2.5-point floor, which cannot exclude a headroom gap large enough to manufacture the ~4-point DiD they are powered for. Accepting the null as the license for the causal claim is the design's central logical gap. (b) Power vs. the phenomenon: the DiD is a second difference whose first difference is the marginal value of *one* injected item at k=1. The proposal's own motivating pilot reports that a *full seven-item* bank moved only six to seven items; a one-item first difference is therefore on the order of a point, and its second difference smaller still, against a stated MDE of ~4 points. By the authors' own reporting rule ('positive point estimate with CI covering zero is reported as inconclusive'), the modal outcome of the load-bearing prediction P2 is pre-registered to be unresolvable — meaning the paper's stated delta over MemMachine is, in expectation, not delivered. A secondary version of the same complaint hits P1: 'argmax-k moves from {4,8} to {0,1,2}' is an argmax over five cells each carrying roughly ±2.5-point uncertainty, and if the k-curve under I3 is simply flat (the most likely outcome if memory is worthless there), the argmax lands in the predicted low set by chance a large fraction of the time. That is a coin flip dressed as a pre-registration; only the mixed-effects interaction is a defensible estimand.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: Invert the manipulation and move the power there. Instead of deleting clauses from the instruction, delete the instruction-duplicating span *from the memory item*: inject m* intact vs. m* with its duplicating sentence removed vs. m* with a length-matched non-duplicating sentence removed, all under the identical full instruction I3-s1. This tests exactly the same relational proposition (does the harm live in the overlap?) but holds instruction quality, length, and task difficulty perfectly fixed, so there is no headroom confound and no need for an underpowered B0/C0 equivalence gate. It can also be run at k=4 or k=8, where the aggregate effect is an order of magnitude larger than a single item's marginal value, instead of at k=1 where it is invisible. Make this E4-prime the primary experiment and demote the grid to context. Then: (1) reallocate the 18 conditional Tier-3 passes and, if needed, shrink E1 to fund n in the low thousands for the mechanism test — passes are only ~2,400 generations, so power here is bought cheaply; (2) if the instruction-side knockout is kept, adjudicate B0 vs C0 with a TOST equivalence test at a pre-specified margin derived from the DiD's MDE, not by failure to reject, and pre-register a headroom-matched reweighting; (3) make the mixed-effects interaction the sole primary for P1 and report argmax-k descriptively only; (4) add the instruction-side length placebo named below.
reviews.missing_baseline: An instruction-side length/specificity placebo: an instruction matched to I3-s1 in token count, register, and apparent specificity but containing none of *this* task's procedure — e.g. verbose generic reasoning boilerplate, or the optimized instruction for a foreign task. E1 as written confounds 'the instruction contains this task's procedural clauses' with 'the instruction is longer and pushes total context up', and the dilution placebo in E2 pads the *memory*, not the instruction, so it does not address this. I_H does not either: it is a strong, genuinely task-procedural instruction, so it separates 'GEPA artifact' from 'procedural content' but not 'procedural content' from 'more instruction tokens'. Without this arm, the headline negative interaction has an unrun rival explanation that costs two passes to eliminate. Second omission, less central but a reviewer will ask: the item-side redundancy-stripping ablation described above — its absence is conspicuous precisely because it is cheaper, better powered, and more direct than the instruction-side knockout that was chosen instead.
reviews.preprint_collision: The check is empty and the proposal says so plainly: the search tool failed on every attempt and this round contributes no new evidence. The honesty is genuinely creditable and I do not penalize it as misconduct — but by the standard this track sets, an unsearched claim of novelty is a weakness, not a neutral, and it must be scored as one. All carried-forward evidence comes from an earlier five-query capped search, which is thin coverage for a fast-moving area, and none of the five named collision-relevant queries ('instruction-conditioned redundancy', 'prompt optimization x retrieval budget', 'clause-level context ablation', 'sub-additivity in-context', 'memory injection budget agent') has actually been run. The proposal concedes the decisive point itself: if MemMachine or a successor already contains a clause-level or item-level causal test, the proposal collides and should not be run in its current form — and nothing in the submission establishes that it does not. The risk is not hypothetical: chunk-level redundancy filtering (arXiv:2604.24334) plus the FILCO/RECOMP lineage is already moving toward conditioning context admission on what the rest of the prompt contains, and 'redundancy against the instruction' is the obvious next step for that line, so an unseen preprint on the gating idea is materially likely. The commitment to a >=15-query uncapped search before submission is the correct remedy but arrives after the decision this review has to make, and it leaves the reviewer with no way to verify the one claim the paper's value now rests on. As submitted, novelty is asserted, not established.

reviews.one_line_contribution: A clause-level causal test of the claim that an optimizer-evolved instruction and a retrieved memory item are informational substitutes rather than complements: deleting the one instruction clause a memory item duplicates should restore that item's marginal value while deleting a length-matched unrelated clause should not, with the accuracy-optimal memory-injection budget k* predicted to collapse as the instruction absorbs procedural content.
reviews.closest_prior_work: MemMachine (arXiv:2604.04853), which the authors themselves name: it already reports that prompt design and retrieval depth must be co-optimized and that prompt choice changes retrieval's marginal value across depths. That is the substitution *observation*, so E1's interaction test — the proposal's largest and best-powered experiment — is confirmatory of something already on record. The proposal concedes this and relocates its novelty entirely into E4 (clause knockout), which is by its own power analysis the weakest test in the plan (MDE ~4 points on a second difference). Secondarily, arXiv:2412.15266 ('On the Structural Memory of LLM Agents') already establishes flat/plateauing K-curves, which makes the 'high-k regime {4,8}' half of P1 empirically shaky before the grid is run; and MIPROv2 already formalizes prompt = instructions + demonstrations with a searched demonstration count, so the framing (not the interaction measurement) is not new. Redundancy gating itself is explicitly conceded to FILCO/RECOMP/MMR, correctly. Net: novelty is one experiment deep, and that experiment is the underpowered one.
reviews.strongest_objection: E4, the load-bearing mechanism test, contains an internal contradiction between its prediction (P2) and its own pre-registered confound gate. Substitution predicts m* gains marginal value under the targeted knockout B (= I3 minus clause c(m*)) because m* now supplies information the instruction no longer carries. But information can only be restored if it was worth something: if c(m*) contributes X accuracy points at k=0, then B0 is worse than A0 by ~X, and the recoverable DiD is bounded above by ~X. The gate demands that B0 and C0 be 'indistinguishable within the noise floor' — i.e. that X be smaller than the noise floor — which caps the true DiD *below the noise floor* and far below the stated MDE of ~4 points. So the two outcomes are: the gate passes and the DiD is guaranteed null by construction (reported as 'refuted' or 'underpowered'), or the DiD is large enough to detect and the gate almost certainly fails, at which point the authors have pre-committed to declaring it confounded. Either way E4 cannot confirm P2. The confound is not incidental: c(m*) is selected as the clause most duplicated by a retrieved item for *this query*, i.e. the most query-relevant clause, while c' is selected as a clause no retrieved item duplicates, i.e. the least query-relevant clause. B and C are matched on length but systematically anti-matched on relevance. A secondary version of the same objection: even if a positive DiD survives, it is equally well explained by 'memory can supply procedure the instruction is missing' — a far weaker and less interesting claim than instruction-conditioned redundancy — because nothing in the design distinguishes m* restoring *the specific duplicated content* from m* restoring *any* removed query-relevant procedure. Layered on top: the proposal's own pilot evidence (7 items harmed, 3 items did not, under a non-optimized instruction) already implies argmax-k is low under a minimal instruction, which contradicts P1's premise that argmax-k sits in {4,8} under I0 and would render the pre-registered 'regime shift' unobservable; and the E1 gate (I3 must beat I0 at k=0 beyond the noise floor) is likely to fire, since the track's own prior result is that prompt evolution fixed as many items as it broke and moved only the class-balanced metric.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: (1) Rebuild E4 as a dose-response rather than a binary knockout: pre-measure each clause's standalone k=0 contribution on a held-out split, then predict that the DiD scales with the measured clause effect. This replaces the self-defeating 'B0 must equal C0' gate with the correct control (regress item-recovery on clause-importance, and show recovery exceeds what a non-duplicating item recovers from the same clause deletion). (2) Match B and C on query-relevance, not just token length — the placebo clause must be one that is query-relevant but duplicated by no retrieved item, and its standalone effect must be matched to c(m*)'s; also replace deletion with neutral-filler substitution so instruction length is held constant. (3) Add the arm that actually isolates relational redundancy: under the targeted knockout B, inject a *non-duplicating* item of matched retrieval score. Substitution requires m* to recover more than that item does; 'memory fills any instruction gap' predicts they recover equally. (4) Add the missing instruction-side length placebo (below). (5) Drop argmax-k as a pre-registered confirmatory statistic — it is an argmax over five noisy point estimates with no stated inferential procedure and no CI; fit k* from the interaction model with a bootstrap CI instead. (6) Execute the collision search before submission rather than committing to it, and reduce the primary grid (E1 duplicates MemMachine's observation) to fund the mechanism arms above.
reviews.missing_baseline: An instruction-side length/content placebo: I0 plus length-matched, topically plausible but procedurally empty instruction text, matched to I3-s1's token count, evaluated across the same k grid. As written, every step of the ladder (I0 -> I1 -> I3, and I_H, which is a *strong* instruction and so cannot serve as neutral filler) confounds procedural content with instruction length, and longer instructions change where memory items sit in the context window and how much attention budget they get. E2 pads only the *memory* slot, so the entire lost-in-the-middle / prompt-length explanation of the negative interaction is untested on the axis where it actually operates. A reviewer would also demand a random-bank control — real memory items sampled off-query at matched k — to separate 'any injected item costs interference' from 'instruction-duplicating items cost interference'; E2's synthetic padding is not a substitute for real-but-non-duplicating retrieved text.
reviews.preprint_collision: Weak, and the proposal says so itself: the search tool failed on every attempt and *zero queries were executed this round*, so the submission contains no executed novelty search. Per the standard that an unsearched claim of novelty is a weakness rather than a neutral, this alone justifies a markdown. The carried-forward evidence is a five-query capped search flagged as provisional, and the authors explicitly write that if MemMachine or a successor already contains a clause-level or item-level causal test, 'this proposal collides and should not be run in its current form' — that is an unresolved, self-identified collision risk in the fastest-moving corner of this literature (2026 context-curation, memory-budget, and instruction-retrieval-interaction preprints appear monthly). I was not able to verify the cited identifiers independently, and most are given as bare arXiv numbers (2604.27003, 2604.27283, 2603.02473, 2604.24334) without titles or authors, which makes them uncheckable as written and would draw a request for full citations. Credit where due: the honesty is exemplary and the commitment to a >=15-query search plus a partial-collision fallback design is the right response — but a commitment to search is not a search, and the novelty score reflects an unestablished, not a disproven, novelty claim.
